analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal spending to expand immigration detention and adds independent oversight of detention facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced by a single senator with zero cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Homeland Security Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the Department of Homeland Security from using federal money to build or expand immigration detention facilities, and would require the department's Inspector General to make unannounced inspections, audit facilities for compliance with standards on sexual abuse and medical care, and investigate deaths in custody. Facilities judged inadequate twice could lose their contracts. It also directs DHS to produce a plan for cutting detention beds in half and using cheaper, community-based alternatives.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants held in detention and their families, who would gain independent inspections, investigations of deaths and medical neglect, and public reporting of complaints. Taxpayers would also benefit, since the bill cites community-based supervision programs that operated at a fraction of detention's cost with near-total compliance [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits DHS from using federal funds to construct or expand immigration detention facilities, and requires a plan to cut detention beds to 50 percent of fiscal 2018 levels while implementing community-based alternatives [S2][S3].

Requires the DHS Inspector General to conduct unannounced annual inspections, audits, and investigations into deaths in custody, medical and mental health care, sexual assault, and attorney access — and to publish the results publicly [S2][S3].

Bars DHS from continuing contracts with any facility deemed inadequate in its two most recent inspections or investigations, and requires the department's civil rights office to investigate complaints and publish data quarterly [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit detention contractors and any entity that profits from new detention contracts, which would lose access to construction and expansion spending; DHS would also bear the cost of new oversight, with about $55 million per year authorized for inspections and civil rights investigations through 2028 [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill restricts expansion through the budget without changing the detention-bed levels Congress sets each year in appropriations bills, which could create a conflict between the moratorium and the number of beds the department is funded to fill [S3].

It authorizes roughly $55 million a year through 2028 for inspections and civil rights investigations, a new ongoing cost, and reduces detention capacity without itself funding the community-based alternatives it directs DHS to plan for [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The oversight provisions address documented problems — the bill's own findings cite more than 170 deaths in detention since 2003 and few investigations of abuse complaints — and community supervision is far cheaper than detention, so the main costs fall on detention contractors and on DHS's budget. The main design weakness is that the moratorium operates alongside, but does not change, the annual appropriations bed mandate, which could blunt its effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced the Detention Oversight, Not Expansion Act on July 23, 2019 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which was its last action [S5].
No senator cosponsored the bill, and it received no further action in the 116th Congress [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit detention operators and DHS's existing detention practices, which continued unimpeded; the independent inspection regime the bill proposed never took effect.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee; the bill's only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: The 53 Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate majority party of the 116th Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of any party; it sat in a committee chaired by a Republican and never advanced.

industries.industry: For-profit detention facility operators (private prison contractors)
industries.note: The bill would ban new contracts, expansions, and riders that increase detention beds — the main growth channel for private detention operators — and could terminate contracts with facilities judged inadequate twice. These contractors hold the majority of ICE detention beds, so a moratorium directly limits their revenue growth.

industries.industry: Government contractors running ICE inspection and compliance work
industries.note: The bill replaces ICE's in-house self-inspections — which its findings say rarely flagged problems before and after deaths — with independent Inspector General oversight, shifting that work and about $55 million a year to oversight functions.

industries.industry: Community-based case management and nonprofit legal and shelter services
industries.note: The bill directs DHS to plan for community-based alternatives to detention developed with nonprofit legal service and shelter providers, citing a terminated case-management program that cost a fraction of detention with near-100 percent compliance.
